title: Infra IaC Modules and CI/CD Guidelines for GPU Fleet and Networking
author: Ayesha Patel
body:
Purpose
This document defines Redwood Inference engineering standards for Terraform/IaC modules and CI/CD pipelines that manage GPU fleet capacity, cloud accounts and networking, and related infra runbooks. The goal is consistent, auditable changes across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments while minimizing blast radius and supporting fast iteration for engineering teams.

Scope
- Terraform module conventions and catalog for common infra primitives (VPC, subnets, routing, IAM, GPU node pools, autoscaling groups, cluster bootstrap).
- CI/CD pipeline requirements for plan/apply, security gating, and automated tests.
- Networking patterns for cross-account VPC peering, transit gateways, and private endpoints used by the runtime.
- Runbook links and operational requirements for capacity changes and incident rollback.

Ownership and Contacts
- Doc owner: infra platform (owner_team: engineering).
- Primary maintainers: infra-iac team (Slack: #infra-iac).
- Oncall for changes: infra-sre rotation (see /confluence/eng-sre/oncall-and-incident-response).

Design Principles
1) Small, composable modules: each Terraform module should do one thing (e.g., vpc, subnet, gpu-node-pool, kms-key). Reuse modules across customers/environments.
2) Explicit interfaces: modules must define a minimal set of inputs and explicit outputs. Avoid implicit provider-side side effects.
3) Idempotence and safe apply: all modules must be safe to plan/apply repeatedly; destructive actions require explicit variable guards.
4) Environment parity: dev/staging/prod modules should be parameterized rather than forked.
5) Access control: use centralized IAM modules and avoid ad-hoc inline policies.

Module Catalog (recommended modules)
- core/vpc: VPC, public/private subnets, route tables, NAT gateways, DNS zones.
- core/network-connectivity: TGW/Transit, VPC peering helpers, VPN attachment module.
- security/iam: role templates, assume role patterns, managed policies, permission boundaries.
- security/kms: KMS key provisioning, aliasing, rotation policy.
- compute/gpu-node-pool: GPU instance ASG/managed node group with spot/fallback profiles, instance types list, GPU-specific bootstrapping (NVIDIA drivers, cuda, container runtime).
- compute/gpu-autoscaler: autoscaling policy, cluster-autoscaler integration, scale-down TTLs.
- storage/object-store: S3 buckets, lifecycle, encryption, endpoint policies.
- platform/eks-cluster: EKS cluster bootstrap, OIDC provider, nodegroup wiring.
- observability/logging: CloudWatch/Datadog log groups, metric namespaces, retention.

Module Naming and Versioning
- Module directory names must use kebab-case and be prefixed by category (e.g., compute/gpu-node-pool).
- Semantic versioning: follow MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Bump MAJOR for breaking API changes.
- Registry: publish stable module versions to the internal registry (artifact repo) and reference by version in environment roots.

Module Interface Standards
All modules must include the following top-level variables and outputs (examples):
- Required variables: name_prefix, environment, region, owner_tag, tags (map).
- Optional variables: enable_deletion_protection (boolean), extra_tags (map), allowed_cidrs (list).
- Outputs: resource_ids (list), primary_subnet_ids (list), iam_role_arn (string), connection_endpoints (map).

Example: gpu-node-pool module usage
```hcl
module "gpu_node_pool" {
  source           = "git::ssh://git.example.com/infra/modules/compute/gpu-node-pool.git?ref=v1.2.0"
  name_prefix      = "redwood-gpu"
  environment      = "prod"
  region           = "us-west-2"
  instance_types   = ["p4d.24xlarge", "g5.12xlarge"]
  desired_capacity = 10
  max_capacity     = 40
  spot_percentage  = 30
  owner_tag        = "eng-serving-runtime"
}
```

Parameter and Secret Handling
- Do not hardcode secrets or raw credentials in modules. Use KMS-encrypted SSM Parameter Store or secrets manager modules.
- Modules may reference KMS keys by arn (output from security/kms module).
- For bootstrap scripts that require secrets, use instance profile roles with short-lived tokens and fetch at bootstrap time.

CI/CD Pipeline Standards
All IaC changes must flow through the standard CI/CD pipeline with these checks:
1) Pre-merge checks (PR): format (terraform fmt), static validation (tflint), security checks (checkov or tfsec), module unit tests (terratest or kitchen-terraform).
2) Plan on PR: create and post a terraform plan artifact in the PR, clearly labeled with changed resources and diff summaries.
3) Manual approval gate for prod: any plan that affects production GPU capacity, networking (route table, TGW), or IAM must require at least one approver from infra-sre and one from security.
4) Automated apply: merges to non-prod branches trigger an automated apply step (with auto-approve) only if plan passes. Prod applies require a gated workflow that records approver metadata.
5) Drift detection: scheduled pipeline to run terraform plan weekly on prod roots and alert on drift.

Example GitHub Actions snippet (plan -> comment -> apply guard)
```yaml
name: Terraform CI
on: [pull_request, push]
jobs:
  fmt-and-validate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Setup Terraform
        uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v2
      - name: terraform fmt
        run: terraform fmt -check -recursive
      - name: tflint
        run: tflint --init && tflint
  plan:
    needs: fmt-and-validate
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Terraform Plan
        run: terraform plan -out=plan.out && terraform show -json plan.out > plan.json
      - name: Comment Plan
        uses: marocchino/action-comment@v1
        with:
          body: |
            Terraform plan for ${{ github.ref }}
            (plan summary attached as artifact)
```

Security and Compliance Gates
- IAM: all new roles and policies must be reviewed by security (label policy-review).
- KMS: keys must be created with least-privilege key policy and key rotation enabled.
- Network ACL and Security Groups: deny by default, explicit allow rules only. Document allowed CIDR ranges per environment.
- Audit logging: module templates must enable resource-level audit logs and forward to the centralized observability pipeline.

GPU Fleet Capacity and Autoscaling Guidelines
- Headroom target: maintain 20% spare GPU capacity (headroom) in prod to handle bursty traffic and model failovers. Monitor with metric: gpu/pool/available_percent.
- Autoscaler config: prefer conservative scale-up (scale-up step: +25% of current capacity, min +1 node) and aggressive scale-down cooldown of 15m.
- Spot fallback policy: configure node pools with primary spot ASG + fallback on-demand nodegroup. Fallback triggers: spot unavailability > 10% sustained for 5m.
- Capacity change process: any planned increase > 20% requires a capacity runbook and QBR notification to SRE. For increases >= 50%, schedule a capacity validation window and smoke tests.

Networking Patterns
- Account topology: use one network account per region per environment (prod-us-west-2, prod-us-east-1). Use centralized transit account for cross-region connectivity.
- Private endpoints: expose internal runtime APIs via PrivateLink endpoints and use route53 private hosted zones per VPC.
- Egress: enforce NAT gateway consolidation per AZ to control costs; use egress auditing for large data flows.

Runbooks and Operational Playbooks
Summary of runbook links:
- GPU capacity runbook: /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/gpu-capacity-and-infra-runbook-2026
- Terraform apply emergency rollback: /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/terraform-apply-rollback-playbook-2026 (create if missing).
- Network incident triage: /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/network-incident-triage-2025

Quick runbook: Emergency rollback of a Terraform apply that impacted GPU node pools
1) Identify the offending PR and plan artifact.
2) If apply just finished, run terraform state list to identify changed resources.
3) If new ASG/nodegroup caused disruption, scale down newly created nodegroup to zero and scale original nodegroup to previous desired capacity.
4) If route changes caused outage, re-apply previous root module state from the latest successful plan (artifact) and notify infra-sre pager.
5) Open incident and run postmortem template (link in incident response).

Testing and Validation
- Unit tests: each module must have unit tests covering variable validation and common failure modes. Use terratest or kitchen-terraform.
- Integration tests: environment-level integration test that provisions a small replica of the GPU stack in ephemeral account/region and runs smoke tests.
- Canary applies: staged canary applies (non-prod -> staging -> prod) with automated traffic smoke tests for runtime endpoints.

Change Management and Rollouts
- Small changes first: prefer many small, reversible changes over large sweeping changes.
- Canary period: after applying to staging, wait for 24-72 hours of stability and pass smoke tests before prod.
- Change log: all applies must include a CHANGELOG entry describing intent, rollback steps, and owner contact.

Audit and Observability Requirements
- Plan artifacts and approval metadata must be stored for at least 90 days in the infra artifact store.
- Apply events must emit metric: infra.apply.count with labels {environment, module, outcome}.
- Drift detection alerts route to #infra-ops with runbook link.

Onboarding Checklist for New Modules
1) Add module to internal registry and create README with inputs/outputs and example usage.
2) Add unit and integration tests and CI workflow.
3) Add to module ownership table (README/OWNERS).
4) Schedule a design review with infra-iac and security for IAM/KMS/networking implications.

Appendix: Example Terraform variable conventions
| Variable name | Type | Description | Required | Example |
| name_prefix | string | Resource name prefix | yes | redwood-gpu |
| environment | string | env tag (dev/staging/prod) | yes | prod |
| owner_tag | string | team owner | yes | eng-serving-runtime |
| allowed_cidrs | list(string) | CIDRs allowed to access service | no | ["10.0.0.0/8"] |
